seo.title: Critical Security Mistakes Blockchain Engineers Make
seo.description: Learn from common security mistakes in blockchain infrastructure. Avoid consensus bugs, P2P vulnerabilities, and cryptographic implementation errors.

content.intro: A single bug in blockchain infrastructure can compromise an entire network. These mistakes have caused chain splits, fund losses, and network outages. Learn from them.

items.description: Using operations that produce different results on different machines: floating point, unordered maps, system time.
items.impact: Different nodes compute different state. Chain split. Network partition.
items.prevention: Audit all code paths for determinism. No floats, ordered data structures only, use block time.
items.example: Using HashMap instead of BTreeMap in Rust, causing different iteration order on different machines.
items.title: Nondeterministic state transitions

items.description: Fork choice rule that does not match specification or has edge case bugs.
items.impact: Nodes follow different chains. Network cannot reach consensus.
items.prevention: Extensive testing against spec test vectors. Fuzzing fork choice code.
items.example: Tie-breaking rule for equal-weight forks that differs between clients.
items.title: Incorrect fork choice implementation

items.description: Marking blocks as final when they are not, or not finalizing when they should be.
items.impact: Reorging 'final' blocks breaks applications. Not finalizing stalls the chain.
items.prevention: Follow finality specs exactly. Test all finality edge cases.
items.example: Finalizing a block before checking if it has sufficient attestations.
items.title: Finality gadget bugs

items.description: Not slashing validators who violate rules, or slashing innocent validators.
items.impact: Attacks go unpunished or honest validators lose stake.
items.prevention: Implement slashing conditions exactly per spec. Extensive testing.
items.example: Failing to detect double-voting because of timestamp precision issues.
items.title: Slashing condition errors

items.description: Accepting blocks, transactions, or state from peers without cryptographic verification.
items.impact: Malicious peers can corrupt node state. False blocks accepted.
items.prevention: Verify all signatures and proofs. Never trust, always verify.
items.example: Accepting a block header without verifying the proof-of-work or signature.
items.title: Trusting peer data without verification

items.description: Node can be surrounded by attacker peers, isolated from honest network.
items.impact: Attacker controls node's view of the network. Double-spend possible.
items.prevention: Diverse peer selection. Monitor peer behavior. Detect isolation.
items.example: All peer slots filled by attacker-controlled nodes feeding false chain.
items.title: Eclipse attack vulnerability

items.description: Not rate limiting messages, not validating before heavy processing.
items.impact: Network brought down by spam. Nodes crash or fall behind.
items.prevention: Validate cheaply first. Rate limit per peer. Disconnect bad actors.
items.example: Processing full block validation before checking basic header validity.
items.title: Insufficient DoS protection

items.description: Small request triggers large response, enabling DDoS amplification.
items.impact: Attackers use nodes to amplify attacks against other targets.
items.prevention: Limit response sizes. Authenticate requesters when appropriate.
items.example: Responding to getdata requests for hundreds of blocks without limiting.
items.title: Message amplification vulnerabilities

items.description: Implementing cryptographic primitives instead of using audited libraries.
items.impact: Implementation bugs lead to key leakage, forgery, or breaks.
items.prevention: Use established, audited libraries. Have crypto code reviewed.
items.example: Writing your own ECDSA implementation with a timing vulnerability.
items.title: Rolling your own cryptography

items.description: Operations involving secrets that take variable time based on secret values.
items.impact: Timing attacks leak private keys.
items.prevention: Use constant-time comparison and arithmetic for all secret data.
items.example: Comparing signatures byte-by-byte and returning early on mismatch.
items.title: Non-constant-time secret operations

items.description: Using non-cryptographic RNG for key generation or protocol randomness.
items.impact: Predictable keys or protocol values. Complete security break.
items.prevention: Always use cryptographically secure RNG (OS-provided or audited library).
items.example: Using rand() or time-seeded PRNG for generating validator private keys.
items.title: Weak random number generation

items.mistake: Private key exposure in logs or errors
items.description: Accidentally logging private keys or including them in error messages.
items.impact: Private keys leaked to log files or monitoring systems.
items.prevention: Never format private keys as strings. Audit all logging paths.
items.example: Debug log statement that prints the full validator key object.
items.title: Private key exposure in logs or errors

sections.heading: State Management Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in state storage and sync.

items.description: Different clients computing different state roots for same transactions.
items.impact: Chain split. Clients cannot agree on state.
items.prevention: Exhaustive testing. Use execution spec tests. Fuzzing.
items.example: Different padding in Merkle Patricia trie causing different roots.
items.title: State root calculation differences

items.description: Not handling database errors, crashes, or corruption properly.
items.impact: Data corruption. Node unable to sync or stuck.
items.prevention: Use atomic operations. Implement recovery procedures.
items.example: Crash during write leaving database in inconsistent state.
items.title: Unsafe database operations

items.description: Removing historical data that is still needed for reorgs or validation.
items.impact: Node cannot handle reorgs. Unable to provide historical data.
items.prevention: Conservative pruning. Keep sufficient history for max reorg.
items.example: Pruning pre-merge data that archive queries still need.
items.title: Pruning too aggressively

items.description: Downloading state from peers and using it without checking proofs.
items.impact: Malicious peer provides false state. Node operates on corrupted data.
items.prevention: Verify state proofs against block headers from trusted source.
items.example: Snap sync accepting account data without checking against state root.
items.title: State sync without verification

sections.heading: Operations Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in node operations and deployment.

items.description: Admin APIs (send transactions, control node) accessible without auth.
items.impact: Anyone can control the node. Funds stolen.
items.prevention: Firewall admin APIs. Require authentication. Localhost only.
items.example: Running geth with --http and admin APIs enabled on public IP.
items.title: Exposing admin RPC publicly

items.description: Storing validator signing keys on internet-connected machine.
items.impact: Keys stolen if machine compromised. Slashing possible.
items.prevention: Use remote signer or HSM. Air-gapped key storage.
items.example: Validator private key in plaintext config file on cloud VM.
items.title: Validator keys on hot machine

items.description: Running nodes without visibility into their health or behavior.
items.impact: Problems not detected until too late. Missed attestations.
items.prevention: Prometheus metrics. Grafana dashboards. PagerDuty alerts.
items.example: Validator falling behind and missing attestations for hours undetected.
items.title: No monitoring or alerting

items.description: Upgrading nodes without testing the procedure in staging.
items.impact: Botched upgrade takes nodes offline. Missed rewards or slashing.
items.prevention: Test upgrades on testnet. Have rollback plan. Monitor closely.
items.example: Config format change breaks validator on upgrade.
items.title: Untested upgrade procedure

items.description: Ambiguous spec language interpreted differently between clients.
items.impact: Client incompatibility. Network splits during edge cases.
items.prevention: Coordinate with other teams. Use reference tests. Fuzzing against other clients.
items.example: Spec says 'should' but one client treats as 'must', another as optional.
items.title: Spec interpretation differences

items.description: No way to identify or negotiate protocol version between peers.
items.impact: Incompatible clients cannot communicate. Hard fork coordination issues.
items.prevention: Version all protocol messages. Implement negotiation handshake.
items.example: New message format breaks old clients without version check.
items.title: Missing protocol versioning

items.description: Encoding/decoding that differs from specification or other clients.
items.impact: Messages misinterpreted. Invalid blocks created or rejected incorrectly.
items.prevention: Use spec-compliant serialization. Test against cross-client fixtures.
items.example: SSZ encoding with wrong field order, producing different hashes.
items.title: Incorrect serialization

items.description: Gas costs for operations that differ from specification.
items.impact: Different execution results. Out-of-gas at different points.
items.prevention: Follow EIP gas costs exactly. Benchmark actual costs vs charged.
items.example: SSTORE gas calculation edge case differs, causing state divergence.
items.title: Gas metering inconsistencies

items.description: Not validating that values fit within expected ranges.
items.impact: Overflow, underflow, or crashes on malformed input.
items.prevention: Check all input ranges. Use bounded integer types.
items.example: Block number as u32 overflows after 4 billion blocks.
items.title: Missing bounds checks

items.description: Allocating memory based on peer-provided sizes without limits.
items.impact: Memory exhaustion. Node crash. Denial of service.
items.prevention: Cap all allocations. Validate sizes before allocating.
items.example: Peer claims message is 4GB, node tries to allocate buffer.
items.title: Unbounded memory allocation

items.description: Not cleaning up connections, file handles, or memory.
items.impact: Slow degradation. Eventually node fails or slows.
items.prevention: Use RAII patterns. Monitor resource usage. Regular restarts if needed.
items.example: TCP connections from disconnected peers never cleaned up.
items.title: Resource leaks

items.description: Long-running operations blocking critical network handling.
items.impact: Node appears offline. Misses messages. Falls behind.
items.prevention: Async everywhere. Move heavy work to background threads.
items.example: Block verification blocking peer message handling for 10+ seconds.
items.title: Blocking the event loop

items.description: No cap on peer connections allowing resource exhaustion.
items.impact: Too many connections consume resources. Degrades performance.
items.prevention: Set reasonable connection limits. Quality-based peer selection.
items.example: Node accepts 10000 connections, runs out of file descriptors.
items.title: Insufficient connection limits

items.description: Allowing attackers to fill caches with useless data.
items.impact: Legitimate data evicted from cache. Performance drops.
items.prevention: Cache admission policies. Per-peer cache quotas.
items.example: Attacker sends many unique transactions, evicts valid pending txs.
items.title: Cache poisoning

items.description: Not using fuzz testing on parsers and state transitions.
items.impact: Edge case bugs not found until exploited in production.
items.prevention: Fuzz all input parsing. Fuzz state transitions. Coverage-guided fuzzing.
items.example: Malformed RLP crashes node, found only when attacker sends it.
items.title: No fuzzing

items.description: Not testing against other implementations before release.
items.impact: Incompatibilities discovered on mainnet.
items.prevention: Sync against all major clients on testnet. Use Hive testing.
items.example: New release cannot sync with Geth due to encoding difference.
items.title: Insufficient cross-client testing

items.description: Not adding tests for previously found bugs.
items.impact: Old bugs reappear after refactoring.
items.prevention: Add regression test for every bug fix. Never delete tests.
items.example: Fixed consensus bug reappears after performance optimization.
items.title: Missing regression tests

proTips: Profile before optimizing. Intuition about performance bottlenecks is often wrong.
Test consensus changes with network simulations, not just unit tests.
Monitor peer connections and block propagation in production, not just availability.

seo.title: 30 Security Mistakes DeFi Developers Make
seo.description: Avoid these 30 common security mistakes that DeFi developers make. From oracle manipulation to flash loan attacks, learn what leads to exploits.

content.intro: DeFi protocols are high-value targets. These common mistakes have led to billions in losses. Learn from others' failures to build more secure protocols.

sections.heading: Oracle Mistakes
sections.description: Price oracle vulnerabilities that lead to manipulation.

items.title: Using spot prices from DEXes
items.description: Using instantaneous spot prices from AMMs allows flash loan manipulation to move prices within a single transaction.
items.impact: Attackers drain funds through price manipulation
items.prevention: Use Chainlink or TWAP oracles. Never rely on single-block spot prices.

items.title: No staleness check on oracle data
items.description: Using stale oracle prices when Chainlink hasn't updated in hours or days.
items.impact: Incorrect prices lead to bad liquidations or arbitrage
items.prevention: Check updatedAt timestamp. Reject prices older than acceptable threshold.

items.title: Missing oracle fallback
items.description: Protocol breaks completely when primary oracle fails or returns zero.
items.impact: Protocol freeze or incorrect behavior during oracle downtime
items.prevention: Implement fallback oracles or safe failure modes.

items.title: Ignoring oracle decimal differences
items.description: Assuming all Chainlink feeds have 8 decimals when some have different precision.
items.impact: Orders of magnitude errors in price calculations
items.prevention: Always check feed decimals and normalize to consistent precision.

items.title: Single oracle dependency
items.description: Trusting one oracle source without cross-validation for critical operations.
items.impact: Oracle compromise breaks entire protocol
items.prevention: For critical operations, cross-reference multiple oracle sources.

items.title: Governance votes based on current balance
items.description: Allowing votes based on token balance at time of vote enables flash loan governance attacks.
items.impact: Attacker passes malicious proposals with borrowed voting power
items.prevention: Use snapshot voting. Require tokens held for minimum time before voting.

items.title: Rewards based on deposit amount without time lock
items.description: Distributing rewards proportional to deposits without lockup allows flash loan reward stealing.
items.impact: Attackers claim disproportionate share of rewards
items.prevention: Require deposits to be present for multiple blocks before earning rewards.

items.title: Share price manipulation on first deposit
items.description: First depositor can donate tokens to inflate share price, griefing subsequent depositors.
items.impact: Early depositors extract value from later depositors
items.prevention: Implement virtual shares or send initial deposit to dead address.

items.title: Collateral value from manipulable source
items.description: Using AMM liquidity token value based on reserves allows collateral manipulation.
items.impact: Attackers borrow more than collateral is worth
items.prevention: Use manipulation-resistant LP token pricing or don't accept LP as collateral.

items.title: Liquidation triggers based on spot price
items.description: Liquidation decisions using spot prices allow predatory liquidations via price manipulation.
items.impact: Healthy positions liquidated through temporary price manipulation
items.prevention: Use TWAP for liquidation triggers. Add liquidation delay.

items.title: State updates after external calls
items.description: Updating balances or state after making external calls violates checks-effects-interactions.
items.impact: Attacker re-enters and exploits stale state
items.prevention: Always update state before external calls. Use ReentrancyGuard.

items.title: Missing reentrancy guard on withdraw
items.description: Withdraw functions making ETH transfers without reentrancy protection.
items.impact: Classic reentrancy drain attack
items.prevention: Add ReentrancyGuard modifier to all functions with external calls.

items.title: Cross-contract reentrancy blind spots
items.description: Only checking single contract reentrancy when protocol has multiple contracts sharing state.
items.impact: Attacker re-enters through different contract in same protocol
items.prevention: Use global reentrancy lock across all protocol contracts.

items.title: ERC-777 callback reentrancy
items.description: Accepting any ERC-20 without considering ERC-777 tokens have transfer hooks.
items.impact: Reentrancy through token transfer callbacks
items.prevention: Use ReentrancyGuard or whitelist accepted tokens.

items.title: Read-only reentrancy in view functions
items.description: View functions returning stale data when called during reentrancy.
items.impact: External protocols that read state during attack get wrong values
items.prevention: Be aware of what external protocols might read. Document reentrancy behavior.

sections.heading: Math and Logic Mistakes
sections.description: Calculation errors and business logic flaws.

items.title: Division before multiplication
items.description: Order of operations causing precision loss. Dividing before multiplying loses precision.
items.impact: Small amounts round to zero, value leakage over time
items.prevention: Always multiply before divide. Use higher precision intermediates.

items.title: Rounding always favoring users
items.description: Rounding in a direction that allows users to extract dust amounts repeatedly.
items.impact: Slow drain through rounding exploitation
items.prevention: Round in favor of the protocol for withdrawals, in favor of users for deposits.

items.title: Unchecked array operations
items.description: Loops over unbounded arrays that can grow beyond gas limits.
items.impact: Function becomes uncallable, funds stuck
items.prevention: Bound array sizes or use pagination for large datasets.

items.title: Integer overflow in fee calculations
items.description: Fee percentage times amount overflowing before division.
items.impact: Wrong fees charged or underflow to huge values
items.prevention: Check for overflow even with Solidity 0.8. Use unchecked carefully.

items.title: Missing slippage protection
items.description: Swaps without minimum output parameter allowing sandwich attacks.
items.impact: Users receive much less than expected due to MEV
items.prevention: Always include minAmountOut parameter. Let users set slippage tolerance.

items.title: Incorrect share calculations
items.description: Vault share math that allows rounding exploitation or share inflation.
items.impact: Value extraction through share manipulation
items.prevention: Use battle-tested ERC-4626 implementations. Add first depositor protection.

sections.heading: Token Handling Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in handling various token types.

items.title: Assuming all ERC-20s return bool
items.description: Not using SafeERC20 when some tokens (USDT) don't return bool on transfer.
items.impact: Transfers silently fail or revert unexpectedly
items.prevention: Always use SafeERC20 for ERC-20 interactions.

items.title: Not handling fee-on-transfer tokens
items.description: Assuming received amount equals transfer amount for tokens with transfer fees.
items.impact: Accounting errors, potential for exploitation
items.prevention: Calculate actual received amount via balance difference.

items.title: Ignoring token decimals
items.description: Assuming 18 decimals when USDC has 6 and others vary.
items.impact: Off by orders of magnitude in calculations
items.prevention: Query token decimals. Normalize all calculations.

items.title: Approval race condition
items.description: Approving new amount without resetting to zero first for tokens with approval race condition.
items.impact: Approved party can spend old + new allowance
items.prevention: Reset to zero first or use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance.

items.title: Not considering token blocklists
items.description: Ignoring that USDC/USDT can blocklist addresses, breaking protocol flows.
items.impact: Funds stuck if protocol address gets blocklisted
items.prevention: Have contingency for blocklist scenarios. Avoid holding stablecoins long-term.

items.title: Missing access control on critical functions
items.description: Administrative functions without onlyOwner or role checks.
items.impact: Anyone can call admin functions and drain or break protocol
items.prevention: Audit every external/public function. Default to restricted, explicitly open.

items.title: Single key controlling everything
items.description: One EOA can pause, upgrade, and withdraw all funds.
items.impact: Key compromise loses everything
items.prevention: Use multisig for admin functions. Separate roles for different operations.

items.title: No timelock on critical operations
items.description: Upgrades and parameter changes execute immediately without delay.
items.impact: No time for users to react to malicious changes
items.prevention: Add timelock for all critical admin operations.

items.title: Incorrect modifier ordering
items.description: Putting access control modifier after other checks allows bypass in some cases.
items.impact: Access control bypassed via early revert
items.prevention: Access control modifiers should be first in modifier chain.

proTips.tip: Study every DeFi exploit post-mortem. The patterns repeat with variations.
Get multiple audits from different firms. Each auditor catches different issues.
Deploy with low caps first. Increase limits gradually as protocol proves secure.
Have a bug bounty program. Ethical hackers finding bugs is better than malicious ones.
Build monitoring and alerts from day one. Fast response limits damage.

seo.title: Critical Security Mistakes GameFi Developers Make
seo.description: Learn from common security mistakes in GameFi development. Avoid economy exploits, smart contract bugs, and client-side vulnerabilities.

content.intro: GameFi combines traditional game security challenges with blockchain complexity. These mistakes have destroyed game economies and lost player trust. Learn from them.

items.description: Creating tokens without ways to remove them from circulation. Pure emission.
items.impact: Hyperinflation. Token becomes worthless. Economy collapses.
items.prevention: Design meaningful sinks: crafting, upgrades, fees. Balance emissions with burns.
items.example: Play-to-earn game that only emits tokens with no mechanisms to burn them.
items.title: No token sinks

items.description: Reward calculations that can be gamed through unintended strategies.
items.impact: Farmers find optimal exploit strategy. Drain rewards intended for real players.
items.prevention: Model economy before launch. Red team your reward formulas.
items.example: Reward per action without considering that bots can do 1000x actions.
items.title: Exploitable reward formulas

items.description: No limits on how many tokens can be minted in a time period.
items.impact: Exploit that triggers mint floods the economy. Instant inflation spiral.
items.prevention: Rate limits on all minting. Caps per address and globally.
items.example: Bug allows single transaction to mint billions of tokens.
items.title: Uncapped minting

items.description: Not considering that one person can have many accounts/wallets.
items.impact: Rewards meant for many players concentrated in few hands.
items.prevention: Design assuming Sybil attacks. Cap per-wallet rewards.
items.example: Airdrop formula that rewards each wallet equally. Farmers create thousands.
items.title: Ignoring multi-accounting

items.description: Using block.timestamp or blockhash for game randomness.
items.impact: Miners/validators can predict or manipulate outcomes.
items.prevention: Use Chainlink VRF or commit-reveal schemes.
items.example: NFT rarity determined by blockhash. Miners manipulate for rare drops.
items.title: Block hash randomness

items.description: Reward claim functions without reentrancy protection.
items.impact: Attacker drains reward pool by reentering during claim.
items.prevention: Use ReentrancyGuard. Follow checks-effects-interactions.
items.example: claimRewards() sends ETH before updating balance. Reenter and claim again.
items.title: Missing reentrancy guards on rewards

items.description: Upgradeable game contracts where single key can change everything.
items.impact: Single compromise or rug pull can change all game rules.
items.prevention: Multisig for upgrades. Timelock delays. Transparent upgrade process.
items.example: Dev wallet hacked. Attacker upgrades contract to drain all NFTs.
items.title: Upgradeable contracts without safeguards

items.description: Contracts without ability to pause during exploit.
items.impact: Cannot stop ongoing exploit. Damage continues until fix deployed.
items.prevention: Implement pausable pattern. Multi-party control of pause.
items.example: Economy exploit discovered but contracts cannot be paused to stop bleeding.
items.title: No pause mechanism

items.description: Trusting client to report game outcomes, loot, or achievements.
items.impact: Cheaters modify client to claim any outcome. Infinite rewards.
items.prevention: Server-authoritative for all economic outcomes. Client is display only.
items.example: Client reports 'killed boss, give 1000 tokens'. Server trusts it.
items.title: Client-authoritative game state

items.description: Embedding treasury or admin private keys in game client code.
items.impact: Anyone decompiling client gets full admin access.
items.prevention: Admin operations server-side only. Keys never in client.
items.example: Unity game with hardcoded treasury wallet private key in build.
items.title: Admin keys in client

items.description: Game client without protection against memory editing or bots.
items.impact: Widespread cheating. Legit players leave. Economy ruined by botters.
items.prevention: Implement anti-cheat. Server-side validation. Behavioral detection.
items.example: Speed hack lets players complete dungeons 100x faster than intended.
items.title: No anti-cheat

items.description: Client generates transactions with user-controllable parameters not validated server-side.
items.impact: Users modify transaction data to claim unearned rewards.
items.prevention: Server generates transaction data. Sign with backend key.
items.example: Client submits 'claim 1000 tokens' transaction. Server doesn't verify amount.
items.title: Unvalidated transaction parameters

items.description: NFT metadata stored on centralized server without integrity checks.
items.impact: Team can change NFT properties after sale. Rug potential.
items.prevention: IPFS for metadata. On-chain attributes when possible. Immutable after mint.
items.example: NFT stats changed after purchase to nerf valuable items.
items.title: Off-chain metadata tampering

items.description: Contract bugs allowing same asset to exist twice or be minted multiple times.
items.impact: Unique items duplicated. Supply assumptions broken.
items.prevention: Test minting thoroughly. Unique ID constraints.
items.example: Race condition in mint allows two identical 'unique' items.
items.title: Asset duplication bugs

items.description: No consideration for how assets will be traded on secondary markets.
items.impact: Wash trading, market manipulation, royalty evasion.
items.prevention: Design with secondary market in mind. Accept royalty limitations.
items.example: Game economy assumes 10% royalty but marketplaces allow 0%.
items.title: Uncontrolled secondary sales

items.description: Unable to freeze compromised or exploited assets during incidents.
items.impact: Exploited items traded away before team can respond.
items.prevention: Implement freeze functionality with proper governance.
items.example: Duplicated rare item sold 100 times before bug is fixed.
items.title: No asset freezing mechanism

items.description: Sequential or predictable NFT token IDs enabling sniping.
items.impact: Bots snipe rare items by predicting IDs before reveal.
items.prevention: Randomize token ID assignment. Delayed reveal mechanisms.
items.example: Rare items always mint at certain ID ranges. Bots target those.
items.title: Predictable token IDs

items.description: Missing automatic halts when economy metrics go abnormal.
items.impact: Exploits run unchecked until manual intervention.
items.prevention: Automatic pauses when daily volume or minting exceeds thresholds.
items.example: Bot mints 10x normal daily tokens before anyone notices.
items.title: No economic circuit breakers

items.description: Rewards that cannot adjust to player count or token price.
items.impact: Economy death spiral when conditions change.
items.prevention: Dynamic rewards based on treasury health and player metrics.
items.example: Fixed 100 token reward becomes worthless or too valuable.
items.title: Static reward rates

items.description: Not accounting for players with massive resource advantages.
items.impact: Whales dominate. New players cannot compete. Game dies.
items.prevention: Diminishing returns. Activity-based rewards. Catch-up mechanics.
items.example: Top 10 players own 90% of all rewards. Others quit.
items.title: Ignoring whale behavior

items.description: Transaction fees that cannot adapt to network conditions or token value.
items.impact: Fees become prohibitive or negligible, breaking UX or spam protection.
items.prevention: Oracle-based fee adjustment. USD-denominated minimum fees.
items.example: Fixed 10 token fee becomes $1000 when token moons.
items.title: No fee adjustment mechanism

items.description: Reward claims without cooldowns or rate limits.
items.impact: Scripts claim rewards faster than intended, draining pools.
items.prevention: Per-address cooldowns. Global rate limits. Batch claim penalties.
items.example: Bot claims 1000 small rewards per second instead of one big one.
items.title: No rate limiting on claims

items.description: Game asset prices based on single-block AMM state.
items.impact: Flash loans manipulate prices for unfair advantages.
items.prevention: Use TWAPs. Multi-block price averaging. Oracle integration.
items.example: Manipulate token price, buy cheap game items, restore price.
items.title: Flash loan vulnerable pricing

items.description: Trades execute without maximum slippage parameters.
items.impact: Sandwich attacks extract value from player trades.
items.prevention: User-defined slippage limits. MEV protection integration.
items.example: Player swap gets sandwiched, loses 20% to MEV bots.
items.title: No slippage protection

items.description: Game logic relying on block.timestamp for time-sensitive features.
items.impact: Validators manipulate timestamp within allowed range for advantage.
items.prevention: Use block numbers for timing. Accept timestamp variance.
items.example: Daily reset based on timestamp. Validator extends their play window.
items.title: Timestamp manipulation vulnerability

items.description: Reading blockchain state directly in game loop, causing performance issues.
items.impact: Slow game. RPC rate limits. Poor player experience.
items.prevention: Index on-chain data. Cache appropriately. Background sync.
items.example: Game queries NFT ownership on-chain for every frame.
items.title: Trusting on-chain data without indexing

items.description: Game assumes transactions always succeed. No retry or error states.
items.impact: Players lose progress or get stuck when transactions fail.
items.prevention: Handle all transaction states. Retry logic. Clear error messages.
items.example: Player completes level but reward transaction fails silently.
items.title: No transaction failure handling

items.description: Requiring signature for every action. Pop-ups for minor operations.
items.impact: Players frustrated. Abandon game due to wallet fatigue.
items.prevention: Batch transactions. Session keys. Embedded wallets for minor actions.
items.example: Pop-up to sign every item pickup in action game.
items.title: Wallet UX friction

items.description: Not handling chain reorgs or transaction replacements.
items.impact: Game state desyncs from actual on-chain state.
items.prevention: Wait for finality. Handle reorg events. Resync mechanisms.
items.example: Player shows item they no longer own due to reorg.
items.title: Incorrect chain event handling

items.description: Generic error messages that don't help players resolve issues.
items.impact: Players confused and frustrated. Support tickets increase.
items.prevention: Specific error messages with suggested actions.
items.example: 'Transaction failed' instead of 'Insufficient gas for this action'.
items.title: Insufficient error messages

proTips: Playtest your economy with adversarial players before launch.
Token sinks are as important as faucets. Plan both from day one.
Anti-cheat is a continuous effort, not a one-time implementation.

seo.title: 30 Common Mistakes NFT Developers Make (And How to Avoid Them)
seo.description: Learn from the mistakes of others. A detailed guide to the most common errors NFT developers make in smart contracts, metadata, and launch strategy.

content.intro: NFT development combines smart contract security with art, metadata, and launch logistics. Here are the most common mistakes that cost NFT developers money, reputation, or both.

items.title: Using sequential token IDs for reveal
items.description: Predictable token IDs let snipers identify rare NFTs before reveal by watching metadata.
items.solution: Use randomized assignment with Chainlink VRF or commit-reveal schemes.

items.title: No reentrancy protection on mint
items.description: Mint functions with callbacks (like safe transfers) can be exploited for extra mints.
items.solution: Use ReentrancyGuard and checks-effects-interactions pattern.

items.title: Integer overflow in batch minting
items.description: Pre-0.8.0 contracts without SafeMath could overflow mint counters.
items.solution: Use Solidity 0.8+ or implement proper overflow checks.

items.title: Unchecked array lengths in airdrops
items.description: Airdrop functions without length limits can exceed block gas limit.
items.solution: Batch airdrops with reasonable limits per transaction.

items.title: Allowing mints to contracts without callback check
items.description: Minting to non-ERC721Receiver contracts locks tokens permanently.
items.solution: Use safeMint or implement receiver checks.

items.title: Storing allowlist on-chain
items.description: On-chain arrays are expensive and can be manipulated by watching transactions.
items.solution: Use Merkle trees for gas-efficient, tamper-proof allowlists.

items.title: No per-wallet mint limits on allowlist
items.description: Allowlisted addresses can transfer their spot to others or mint multiple times.
items.solution: Track mints per address and enforce limits.

items.title: Merkle proof replay attacks
items.description: Valid proofs can be reused if contract doesn't track used proofs.
items.solution: Mark addresses as claimed after successful mint.

items.title: Allowlist signature without expiry
items.description: Signed allowlist entries without expiry can be used indefinitely.
items.solution: Include expiry timestamp in signed messages.

items.title: Front-runnable signature reveals
items.description: Signatures revealed in pending transactions can be stolen.
items.solution: Tie signatures to specific msg.sender addresses.

items.title: Centralized metadata hosting
items.description: Traditional hosting means metadata disappears if server goes down.
items.solution: Use IPFS, Arweave, or on-chain storage for permanence.

items.title: Mutable metadata without transparency
items.description: Ability to change metadata after mint destroys trust.
items.solution: Use provenance hash and freeze metadata after reveal.

items.title: No provenance hash
items.description: Without provenance, you cannot prove art was finalized before minting.
items.solution: Hash all metadata/images and publish before mint starts.

items.title: Incorrect token URI implementation
items.description: Returning wrong URI format breaks marketplace display.
items.solution: Test on OpenSea testnet before mainnet. Follow metadata standards.

items.title: Large image files
items.description: Large files slow loading and increase IPFS pinning costs.
items.solution: Optimize images. Use proper compression. Consider thumbnails.

items.title: Using block.timestamp for randomness
items.description: Miners can manipulate timestamps within bounds. Not truly random.
items.solution: Use Chainlink VRF for verifiable randomness.

items.title: Predictable blockhash randomness
items.description: blockhash(block.number) is always 0. blockhash of past blocks can be known.
items.solution: Use commit-reveal or Chainlink VRF.

items.title: Single-transaction reveal
items.description: Reveals in same transaction as mint let attackers simulate and cherry-pick.
items.solution: Separate mint and reveal into different transactions/blocks.

items.title: Insufficient randomness entropy
items.description: Combining weak entropy sources doesn't make strong randomness.
items.solution: Use cryptographically secure randomness from oracles.

items.title: Owner can rug-pull funds
items.description: Arbitrary withdrawal functions let owners steal mint proceeds.
items.solution: Use transparent withdrawal to known addresses or multi-sig.

items.title: No withdrawal function
items.description: Forgetting to include a withdrawal function locks ETH in contract forever.
items.solution: Always test withdrawal on testnet before mainnet deploy.

items.title: Single owner key
items.description: One compromised key loses entire collection control.
items.solution: Use multi-sig for owner functions.

items.title: Pausable without unpause
items.description: Some contracts can be paused but have no unpause function.
items.solution: Ensure all pausable functionality can be reversed.

items.title: No on-chain royalty support
items.description: Without EIP-2981, royalties depend on marketplace voluntary enforcement.
items.solution: Implement EIP-2981 royaltyInfo function.

items.title: Immutable royalty recipient
items.description: Cannot update royalty address if wallet is compromised.
items.solution: Make royalty recipient updateable by owner/multi-sig.

items.title: Excessive royalty percentages
items.description: Very high royalties encourage marketplace bypass.
items.solution: Keep royalties reasonable. 5-10% is standard.

items.title: No gas optimization
items.description: High gas costs during popular mints price out regular users.
items.solution: Use ERC721A for batch minting. Optimize storage operations.

items.title: Unverified contract on Etherscan
items.description: Unverified contracts look suspicious and reduce trust.
items.solution: Verify source code immediately after deployment.

items.title: No testnet testing
items.description: Deploying directly to mainnet without thorough testing.
items.solution: Test extensively on Goerli/Sepolia. Test OpenSea display.

items.title: Wrong network deployment
items.description: Accidentally deploying to wrong network or testnet with real funds.
items.solution: Double-check network ID in deployment scripts.

proTips: Deploy a test collection first. Iterate on metadata and minting before the real launch.
Gas optimization matters for minting. Users will compare your mint cost to competitors.
Test with large collection sizes. Bugs often appear at scale.

seo.title: 30 Common Mistakes Smart Contract Auditors Make
seo.description: Avoid these 30 common mistakes that smart contract auditors make. From missing edge cases to report writing errors, improve your audit quality.

content.intro: Even experienced auditors make mistakes that can lead to missed vulnerabilities or inaccurate reports. Learn from these common pitfalls to improve your audit quality.

sections.heading: Preparation Mistakes
sections.description: Errors made before the actual code review begins.

items.title: Not reading the documentation first
items.description: Jumping straight into code without understanding intended behavior leads to false positives and missed business logic bugs.
items.impact: Miss context-dependent vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Spend first 10-15% of audit time on docs, specs, and similar protocol audits.

items.title: Unclear scope definition
items.description: Starting without clear scope leads to wasted time on out-of-scope contracts or missing in-scope dependencies.
items.impact: Inefficient time use and missed vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Get explicit scope confirmation in writing before starting any code review.

items.title: Skipping automated tool runs
items.description: Not running Slither, Mythril, or other tools because you think manual review is sufficient.
items.impact: Miss low-hanging fruit that tools catch instantly
items.prevention: Always run automated tools first. They catch issues you might overlook.

items.title: Not setting up the local environment
items.description: Reviewing code without being able to run tests or write PoCs limits vulnerability verification.
items.impact: Cannot verify findings with proof of concept
items.prevention: Clone repo and get tests passing before deep code review.

items.title: Underestimating audit time needed
items.description: Accepting tight deadlines leads to rushed reviews and missed vulnerabilities.
items.impact: Incomplete audit coverage
items.prevention: Use realistic time estimates. Complex DeFi needs 1000+ lines per day is aggressive.

sections.heading: Technical Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in vulnerability identification and analysis.

items.title: Focusing only on code, not economics
items.description: Missing economic exploits because you only look for code bugs, not incentive manipulation.
items.impact: Miss profitable exploits that don't require code bugs
items.prevention: Model economic attacks. Ask: how would someone profit from manipulating this?

items.title: Missing cross-contract reentrancy
items.description: Only checking for single-contract reentrancy when the protocol has multiple interacting contracts.
items.impact: Miss complex reentrancy paths
items.prevention: Map all external calls and check if any can re-enter other protocol contracts.

items.title: Ignoring external dependencies
items.description: Not reviewing how the contract interacts with external protocols like Uniswap, Aave, or Chainlink.
items.impact: Miss integration vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Review external call assumptions. Check for edge cases in integrated protocols.

items.title: Not testing edge cases
items.description: Only testing happy path scenarios without considering zero values, max values, or empty arrays.
items.impact: Miss boundary condition bugs
items.prevention: Systematically test all boundary conditions in critical functions.

items.title: Misunderstanding protocol assumptions
items.description: Making incorrect assumptions about how the protocol should work without verifying with the team.
items.impact: False positives that waste everyone's time
items.prevention: When unsure, ask the team. Document assumptions in your notes.

items.title: Missing read-only reentrancy
items.description: Not considering that view functions can return stale data during reentrancy.
items.impact: Miss reentrancy that affects external protocols
items.prevention: Check if other protocols read state during external calls.

sections.heading: Analysis Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in vulnerability assessment and severity rating.

items.title: Incorrect severity assessment
items.description: Rating findings too high or too low damages credibility and prioritization.
items.impact: Team ignores valid findings or panics over minor issues
items.prevention: Use consistent severity framework. High/Critical requires fund loss or protocol break.

items.title: Not writing proof of concept
items.description: Reporting theoretical vulnerabilities without proving they're exploitable.
items.impact: Invalid findings that cannot be reproduced
items.prevention: Write PoC for all medium+ findings. If you cannot exploit it, reconsider.

items.title: Missing the root cause
items.description: Reporting symptoms rather than underlying vulnerability leads to incomplete fixes.
items.impact: Fix addresses symptom but root cause remains exploitable
items.prevention: Always identify why the vulnerability exists, not just what it does.

items.title: Duplicate findings from different angles
items.description: Reporting the same underlying issue multiple times as separate findings.
items.impact: Inflated finding count, wastes team time reviewing duplicates
items.prevention: Before adding finding, check if it shares root cause with existing finding.

items.title: Missing attack prerequisites
items.description: Not clearly stating what conditions must exist for the attack to succeed.
items.impact: Overstated severity or invalid findings
items.prevention: Document all prerequisites: timing, capital, permissions, market conditions.

items.title: Ignoring gas costs in attack profitability
items.description: Reporting attacks that are unprofitable after gas costs are considered.
items.impact: Invalid economic exploits
items.prevention: Calculate full attack cost including gas and flash loan fees.

sections.heading: Report Writing Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in documenting and communicating findings.

items.title: Unclear vulnerability descriptions
items.description: Writing descriptions that only make sense to you, not the development team.
items.impact: Team cannot understand or fix the issue
items.prevention: Write for developers who did not audit. Include context and clear steps.

items.title: Missing code references
items.description: Not including specific line numbers and file paths for vulnerable code.
items.impact: Team cannot locate the vulnerable code
items.prevention: Include file path, line numbers, and relevant code snippets.

items.title: Vague recommendations
items.description: Suggesting fixes like 'add validation' without specifying what validation.
items.impact: Team implements incomplete fix
items.prevention: Provide specific, implementable fix recommendations with code examples.

items.title: Not explaining impact clearly
items.description: Technical description without business impact leaves team unsure how to prioritize.
items.impact: Critical issues may be deprioritized
items.prevention: Always explain: what can attacker do, how much can they steal, what breaks.

items.title: Forgetting to verify fixes
items.description: Not reviewing the fixes implemented for your findings.
items.impact: Incomplete or incorrect fixes deploy to mainnet
items.prevention: Review all fix commits. Verify root cause addressed, not just symptom.

items.title: Poor report organization
items.description: Dumping findings without logical organization or executive summary.
items.impact: Stakeholders cannot quickly understand risk exposure
items.prevention: Include executive summary, group by severity, provide statistics.

items.title: Working in isolation without team discussion
items.description: Not discussing potential findings with other auditors leads to missed insights.
items.impact: Lower quality audit, duplicate efforts
items.prevention: Schedule regular sync calls. Discuss interesting code paths and potential issues.

items.title: Not tracking time per area
items.description: Spending too much time on one area while neglecting others.
items.impact: Uneven coverage leaves blind spots
items.prevention: Track time spent per contract or area. Ensure balanced coverage.

items.title: Disclosing vulnerabilities inappropriately
items.description: Sharing findings publicly before the team has patched.
items.impact: Enable exploits, damage reputation, potential legal issues
items.prevention: Follow responsible disclosure. Never share details until fixed.

items.title: Not maintaining finding database
items.description: Each audit starts from scratch without use patterns from past audits.
items.impact: Slower audits, repeated mistakes
items.prevention: Maintain personal database of finding patterns and vulnerable code patterns.

items.title: Skipping the retest phase
items.description: Assuming fixes are correct without verification.
items.impact: Broken or incomplete fixes go to production
items.prevention: Always verify fixes address root cause and don't introduce new issues.

items.title: Ignoring test coverage gaps
items.description: Not reviewing what tests exist and what code paths remain untested.
items.impact: Critical paths may be untested, hiding bugs
items.prevention: Review test coverage. Flag untested code as higher risk.

items.title: Missing cross-protocol interactions
items.description: Auditing in isolation without considering how other protocols might interact.
items.impact: Composability attacks missed
items.prevention: Consider flash loan attack vectors and other protocol interactions.

items.title: Not tracking previous audits
items.description: Failing to review findings from previous audits of the same protocol.
items.impact: Re-introducing old vulnerabilities or missing recurring patterns
items.prevention: Always request and review previous audit reports.

proTips.tip: Keep a checklist of common vulnerabilities and check each one explicitly. Do not rely on memory.
Take breaks. Auditor fatigue causes missed findings. Fresh eyes catch more bugs.
Build relationships with protocol teams. Good communication improves audit quality for everyone.
Study every post-mortem. When a protocol gets exploited, understand exactly what the auditors missed.
Contribute to open-source security tools. Building tools deepens your understanding of vulnerability patterns.

seo.title: 30 Common Mistakes Solana Developers Make (And How to Avoid Them)
seo.description: Learn from the mistakes of others. A detailed guide to the most common errors Solana developers make with accounts, PDAs, and program security.

content.intro: Solana's account model and Rust-based development create unique pitfalls that catch even experienced developers. Here are the most common mistakes and how to avoid them.

items.title: Missing account ownership check
items.description: Not verifying that accounts are owned by expected programs allows attackers to pass fake accounts.
items.solution: Always check account.owner matches expected program ID. Anchor does this automatically with #[account()].

items.title: Not validating account discriminators
items.description: Without discriminator checks, wrong account types can be passed to instructions.
items.solution: Use Anchor's automatic discriminator validation. In native, implement manual type checks.

items.title: Missing signer validation
items.description: Not checking that required accounts have actually signed the transaction.
items.solution: Always verify is_signer for accounts that should authorize the action.

items.title: Trusting account data without validation
items.description: Assuming account data is correctly formatted without deserializing and validating.
items.solution: Always deserialize and validate account data. Handle deserialization errors.

items.title: Not checking account mutability
items.description: Attempting to write to accounts not marked as writable.
items.solution: Mark accounts as writable with #[account(mut)] or is_writable checks.

items.title: Inconsistent PDA seeds
items.description: Using different seeds for derivation and validation causes lookup failures.
items.solution: Centralize seed generation. Use constants for seed strings.

items.title: Not storing bump in account
items.description: Recalculating bump wastes compute units and can fail.
items.solution: Store bump seed in the account data. Pass stored bump for signing.

items.title: Using find_program_address in instruction handlers
items.description: find_program_address is expensive. Calling it repeatedly wastes compute.
items.solution: Derive PDA client-side and pass as account. Verify with create_program_address.

items.title: Wrong program ID in PDA derivation
items.description: Using wrong program ID creates PDAs that can't sign for your program.
items.solution: Always use your program's ID for PDA derivation.

items.title: Seeds too long
items.description: PDA seeds have a maximum total length of 32 bytes.
items.solution: Hash long seeds or restructure to stay under limit.

items.title: Not checking token mint
items.description: Token accounts can hold any SPL token. Not validating mint allows wrong tokens.
items.solution: Always validate token_account.mint matches expected mint.

items.title: Ignoring token decimals
items.description: Calculating amounts without considering decimals leads to wrong values.
items.solution: Always account for token decimals in calculations.

items.title: Not closing empty accounts
items.description: Empty token accounts still cost rent. Not closing them leaks SOL.
items.solution: Close token accounts when emptied to recover rent.

items.title: Wrong token program ID
items.description: Token-2022 uses different program ID than SPL Token.
items.solution: Check token_program matches account.owner.

items.title: Not handling frozen accounts
items.description: Transfers to/from frozen accounts fail silently or with confusing errors.
items.solution: Check account freeze state before transfers.

items.title: Integer overflow/underflow
items.description: Rust's release mode doesn't check for overflow by default.
items.solution: Use checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul for all arithmetic.

items.title: Precision loss in division
items.description: Integer division truncates. Order of operations matters for precision.
items.solution: Multiply before dividing. Use fixed-point math for precision.

items.title: Rounding in wrong direction
items.description: Rounding errors can be exploited over many transactions.
items.solution: Round in favor of the protocol, not the user.

items.title: Using u64 for timestamps
items.description: Solana Clock uses i64 for timestamps. Type mismatch causes issues.
items.solution: Use i64 for timestamp handling. Cast carefully.

items.title: CPI to arbitrary programs
items.description: Not validating target program allows attackers to redirect CPIs.
items.solution: Hardcode expected program IDs or validate against known addresses.

items.title: Missing signer seeds in CPI
items.description: PDA-signed CPIs without seeds fail authorization.
items.solution: Pass correct signer_seeds when PDA needs to sign CPI.

items.title: Reentrancy through CPI
items.description: CPIs can call back into your program with unexpected state.
items.solution: Follow checks-effects-interactions. Update state before CPI.

items.title: Not checking CPI return values
items.description: Ignoring CPI results can mask failures.
items.solution: Always check invoke/invoke_signed results.

items.title: Not handling compute budget
items.description: Complex operations can exceed compute limit.
items.solution: Test compute usage. Request additional compute units if needed.

items.title: Forgetting to update IDL
items.description: Changed program without updating IDL breaks clients.
items.solution: Regenerate IDL after program changes. Version your IDLs.

items.title: Testing only on localnet
items.description: Localnet doesn't have same constraints as mainnet.
items.solution: Test on devnet with realistic conditions.

items.title: Not initializing accounts properly
items.description: Uninitialized accounts contain garbage data.
items.solution: Always initialize account data. Use Anchor's init constraint.

items.title: Ignoring rent requirements
items.description: Accounts below rent-exempt threshold get garbage collected.
items.solution: Ensure accounts have sufficient lamports for rent exemption.

items.title: Clockwork misuse
items.description: Using Solana's clock sysvar for critical timing without considering validator manipulation.
items.solution: Use slot numbers or understand clock manipulation bounds.

items.title: Hardcoded cluster-specific addresses
items.description: Using mainnet program IDs in devnet code or vice versa.
items.solution: Use environment configuration for cluster-specific addresses.

items.title: Ignoring transaction size limits
items.description: Solana transactions have a 1232 byte limit, causing unexpected failures.
items.solution: Monitor transaction sizes. Split large operations across multiple transactions.

proTips: Read the source code of programs you interact with via CPI. Documentation may be outdated.
Test with realistic transaction volumes. Solana programs behave differently under load.
Keep your Anchor version pinned. Breaking changes between versions are common.

seo.title: 30 Common Security Mistakes Solidity Developers Make (And How to Avoid Them)
seo.description: Learn from the most expensive mistakes in smart contract development. This guide covers 30 critical security errors with real-world consequences and fixes.

content.intro: Smart contract bugs have cost billions of dollars. This guide covers the 30 most common security mistakes Solidity developers make, with real-world consequences and concrete solutions to prevent them in your code.

sections.heading: Critical Vulnerabilities
sections.description: These mistakes have led to the largest exploits in DeFi history. Avoiding them is non-negotiable.

items.title: Missing Reentrancy Protection
items.mistake: Making external calls before updating state variables, allowing attackers to re-enter and drain funds.
items.consequence: The DAO hack ($60M), Cream Finance ($130M), and countless others exploited this exact pattern.
items.solution: Always use checks-effects-interactions pattern AND ReentrancyGuard. Update all state before external calls.

items.title: Unchecked External Call Returns
items.mistake: Ignoring return values from low-level calls like.call().delegatecall(), or.send().
items.consequence: Failed transfers silently succeed, leading to accounting errors and fund loss.
items.solution: Always check return values: (bool success, ) = addr.call{value: amount}(""); require(success);

items.title: Oracle Price Manipulation
items.mistake: Using spot prices from AMMs without TWAP or multiple oracle sources.
items.consequence: Attackers use flashloans to manipulate prices within a single transaction. Hundreds of millions lost.
items.solution: Use Chainlink or other decentralized oracles. For AMM prices, use TWAP with sufficient window.

items.title: Missing Access Control
items.mistake: Leaving admin functions without proper onlyOwner or role-based modifiers.
items.consequence: Anyone can call privileged functions, drain funds, or take over the contract.
items.solution: Use OpenZeppelin's AccessControl or Ownable2Step. Audit every external/public function.

items.title: Uninitialized Proxy Implementation
items.mistake: Deploying upgradeable contracts without calling the initializer or protecting it.
items.consequence: Attackers call initialize() and become owner. Wormhole lost $320M to a variant of this.
items.solution: Call _disableInitializers() in the constructor and ensure initialize is called during deployment.

items.title: Delegatecall to Untrusted Contract
items.mistake: Using delegatecall with a user-controlled address, allowing arbitrary code execution.
items.consequence: Attacker executes malicious code in your contract's context, taking full control.
items.solution: Never delegatecall to addresses that users can influence. Whitelist allowed targets.

items.title: tx.origin for Authorization
items.mistake: Using tx.origin instead of msg.sender for access control.
items.consequence: Phishing attacks can trick users into calling malicious contracts that relay to yours.
items.solution: Always use msg.sender for authorization. tx.origin should almost never be used.

items.title: Missing Slippage Protection
items.mistake: Not allowing users to specify minimum output amounts in swaps or deposits.
items.consequence: Sandwich attacks extract value from every transaction. Users lose to MEV bots.
items.solution: Add minAmountOut parameters to all trading functions. Let users set their slippage tolerance.

items.title: Integer Overflow in Pre-0.8 Solidity
items.mistake: Using Solidity <0.8 without SafeMath library for arithmetic operations.
items.consequence: Overflows wrap around, allowing attackers to create tokens from nothing or bypass checks.
items.solution: Use Solidity 0.8+ or SafeMath for all arithmetic. Be careful with unchecked blocks.

items.title: Insufficient Validation of Merkle Proofs
items.mistake: Not validating that Merkle leaves are formatted correctly, allowing proof reuse.
items.consequence: Attackers claim multiple times or claim on behalf of others.
items.solution: Hash leaves with abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, amount) and mark claimed addresses.

sections.heading: Major Security Issues
sections.description: These mistakes are frequently exploited and can lead to significant fund loss.

items.title: Using transfer() or send() for ETH
items.mistake: Using.transfer() or.send() which forward only 2300 gas, failing on some contracts.
items.consequence: Transfers to contracts with receive() functions that need more gas will fail permanently.
items.solution: Use.call{value: amount}("") with reentrancy protection instead.

items.title: Hardcoded Gas Values
items.mistake: Hardcoding gas amounts that may become insufficient after EVM upgrades.
items.consequence: Functions become unusable after gas repricing, potentially locking funds.
items.solution: Avoid hardcoded gas values. Test with different gas prices and EVM versions.

items.title: Unsafe Type Casting
items.mistake: Casting between types without checking for truncation (e.g., uint256 to uint128).
items.consequence: Large values get truncated, leading to incorrect calculations and potential exploits.
items.solution: Use SafeCast library or explicit bounds checking before downcasting.

items.title: Missing Zero Address Check
items.mistake: Not validating that critical addresses (owner, fee recipient) aren't address(0).
items.consequence: Funds sent to zero address are burned. Ownership set to zero address locks the contract.
items.solution: Add require(addr != address(0)) for all address parameters in setters and constructors.

items.title: Signature Replay Attacks
items.mistake: Not including nonces or chainId in signed messages, allowing reuse across chains/transactions.
items.consequence: Valid signatures can be replayed, allowing unauthorized actions.
items.solution: Use EIP-712 with chainId and per-user nonces. Increment nonce after each use.

items.title: Block Timestamp Manipulation
items.mistake: Relying on block.timestamp for precise timing in high-stakes situations.
items.consequence: Miners can manipulate timestamp by several seconds, affecting outcomes.
items.solution: Use block numbers for precision. Allow ~15 second tolerance for timestamp-based logic.

items.title: Front-Running Vulnerable Approvals
items.mistake: Changing ERC20 allowance without first setting to zero.
items.consequence: Attacker front-runs and spends both old and new allowance.
items.solution: Use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance or set to 0 first, then new value.

items.title: Denial of Service via Block Gas Limit
items.mistake: Writing loops that iterate over unbounded arrays.
items.consequence: Array grows until processing exceeds block gas limit, permanently bricking the contract.
items.solution: Use pagination, caps, or pull patterns instead of push patterns with loops.

items.title: Incorrect Inheritance Order
items.mistake: Wrong order of inherited contracts leading to unexpected function resolution.
items.consequence: Wrong implementation gets called, potentially bypassing security checks.
items.solution: List base contracts from most base-like to most derived. Test inheritance carefully.

items.title: Storage Collision in Upgrades
items.mistake: Changing storage layout between proxy upgrades, corrupting existing data.
items.consequence: Variables point to wrong storage slots, leading to data corruption and exploits.
items.solution: Only append new variables. Use storage gaps. Run upgrade-safety checks.

sections.heading: Common Code Quality Issues
sections.description: These mistakes may not directly cause exploits but indicate poor security practices.

items.title: Using Floating Pragma
items.mistake: Using pragma solidity ^0.8.0 instead of a fixed version.
items.consequence: Contract may compile with untested compiler version introducing bugs.
items.solution: Lock pragma to specific version you've tested: pragma solidity 0.8.20;

items.title: Missing Events for State Changes
items.mistake: Not emitting events when critical state variables change.
items.consequence: Makes monitoring and debugging difficult. Hides malicious admin actions.
items.solution: Emit events for all state changes, especially in admin functions.

items.title: Public Functions That Should Be External
items.mistake: Using public visibility when external would suffice.
items.consequence: Wastes gas and signals lack of attention to detail in security reviews.
items.solution: Use external for functions only called from outside. Reserve public for internal calls.

items.title: Unused Return Values
items.mistake: Calling functions without using their return values.
items.consequence: May miss important status information or error conditions.
items.solution: Either use the return value or explicitly discard: (, uint b) = func();

items.title: Missing NatSpec Documentation
items.mistake: Not documenting functions, parameters, and security assumptions.
items.consequence: Makes auditing harder, increases chance of misuse by integrators.
items.solution: Add @notice, @param, @return, and @dev tags to all external functions.

items.title: Using ecrecover Directly
items.mistake: Using raw ecrecover without handling edge cases and malleability.
items.consequence: Signature malleability can lead to duplicate valid signatures.
items.solution: Use OpenZeppelin's ECDSA library which handles all edge cases.

items.title: Inconsistent Error Handling
items.mistake: Mixing require, revert, and assert without clear purpose.
items.consequence: assert uses all remaining gas. Confuses intention of error handling.
items.solution: Use require for input validation, assert only for invariants, custom errors for gas efficiency.

items.title: Magic Numbers in Code
items.mistake: Using raw numbers like 10000 for basis points without constants.
items.consequence: Makes code harder to audit and maintain. Easy to introduce errors.
items.solution: Define constants: uint256 constant BASIS_POINTS = 10000;

items.title: Not Using SafeERC20
items.mistake: Calling ERC20 transfer/approve directly without handling non-standard tokens.
items.consequence: Some tokens don't return bool, causing transfers to fail silently.
items.solution: Use OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 for all token interactions.

items.title: Ignoring Compiler Warnings
items.mistake: Deploying contracts with unresolved compiler warnings.
items.consequence: Warnings often indicate real issues that could become vulnerabilities.
items.solution: Treat warnings as errors. Resolve all warnings before deployment.

proTips: Keep a personal 'bugs I've made' document. Reviewing your past mistakes is the fastest way to stop repeating them.
Before every deployment, ask yourself: 'How would I attack this contract if I had unlimited capital for one block?'
Follow audit reports from Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, and Spearbit. Each report teaches you new attack patterns.
Use Foundry's console.log liberally during development, but remove all logs before deployment to save gas.
When you find a bug, don't just fix it. Add a test that would have caught it. Build your test suite from real bugs.

seo.title: 30 Common Mistakes Web3 Frontend Developers Make (And How to Avoid Them)
seo.description: Learn from the mistakes of others. A detailed guide to the most common errors Web3 frontend developers make in wallet integration, state management, and UX.

content.intro: Web3 frontend development has unique challenges around wallet connections, transaction handling, and blockchain state. Here are the mistakes that trip up most developers.

items.title: Assuming wallet is always connected
items.description: Not handling disconnected state leads to crashes and poor UX.
items.solution: Always check connection state. Show appropriate UI for each state.

items.title: Not handling chain switching
items.description: Users switching networks in wallet breaks app if not handled.
items.solution: Listen for chain changes. Prompt users to switch back or adapt UI.

items.title: Only supporting one wallet
items.description: MetaMask-only apps exclude mobile users and hardware wallet users.
items.solution: Use RainbowKit or Web3Modal to support multiple wallets.

items.title: Not persisting connection state
items.description: Users have to reconnect wallet on every page refresh.
items.solution: Use wagmi's auto-connect feature. Store connection preference.

items.title: Blocking UI during wallet prompts
items.description: User cannot do anything while waiting for wallet signature.
items.solution: Show loading state but allow cancellation. Timeout long requests.

items.title: Not showing transaction status
items.description: Users don't know if transaction succeeded, failed, or is pending.
items.solution: Show clear pending, success, and error states. Link to explorer.

items.title: No gas estimation before send
items.description: Transactions fail due to insufficient gas without warning.
items.solution: Simulate transactions before sending. Show estimated gas cost.

items.title: Ignoring transaction reverts
items.description: Silent failures leave users confused about what happened.
items.solution: Catch revert reasons and display human-readable error messages.

items.title: Not handling stuck transactions
items.description: Low gas transactions can hang indefinitely.
items.solution: Provide speedup/cancel options. Link to tools for stuck transactions.

items.title: Displaying raw error messages
items.description: Technical revert strings are meaningless to users.
items.solution: Map common errors to friendly messages. Log technical details.

items.title: Polling too frequently
items.description: Excessive RPC calls hit rate limits and waste resources.
items.solution: Use appropriate polling intervals. use websockets where available.

items.title: Not caching blockchain data
items.description: Re-fetching same data on every render wastes RPC calls.
items.solution: Use TanStack Query with wagmi for smart caching.

items.title: Stale data after transactions
items.description: UI shows old balances/state after user's transaction confirms.
items.solution: Invalidate queries after transaction success. Optimistic updates.

items.title: Mixing local and chain state incorrectly
items.description: Local state can diverge from blockchain causing confusion.
items.solution: Use blockchain as source of truth. Local state for pending only.

items.title: Not handling block reorgs
items.description: Confirmed transactions can be undone in reorgs.
items.solution: Wait for sufficient confirmations for important transactions.

items.title: Exposing private keys in frontend
items.description: Private keys in client-side code can be stolen.
items.solution: Never use private keys in frontend. Use wallet signatures only.

items.title: Not validating input before signing
items.description: Users might sign malicious transactions from manipulated UI.
items.solution: Validate all inputs. Show clear transaction details before signing.

items.title: Trusting URL parameters blindly
items.description: Phishing attacks can manipulate transaction parameters via URL.
items.solution: Validate and sanitize all URL parameters. Confirm with user.

items.title: No phishing protection
items.description: Users can be tricked by lookalike domains.
items.solution: Educate users. Consider ENS/domain verification features.

items.title: Storing sensitive data in localStorage
items.description: localStorage is accessible to any script on the domain.
items.solution: Never store private keys or sensitive tokens in localStorage.

items.title: No mobile responsiveness
items.description: Many users access dApps via mobile wallet browsers.
items.solution: Build mobile-first. Test in MetaMask Mobile, Rainbow, etc.

items.title: Complex onboarding for new users
items.description: Requiring wallet setup immediately loses potential users.
items.solution: Allow browsing without wallet. Consider embedded wallets for onboarding.

items.title: No loading states
items.description: Blockchain operations are slow. Empty states confuse users.
items.solution: Show skeletons and spinners. Explain why operations take time.

items.title: Displaying raw addresses
items.description: 0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0ab3 is unreadable.
items.solution: Show ENS names when available. Truncate addresses (0x742d...0ab3).

items.title: Not explaining gas
items.description: New users don't understand why they need ETH for transactions.
items.solution: Explain gas in simple terms. Show estimated costs in USD.

items.title: Not testing with real wallets
items.description: Mocked wallets behave differently than MetaMask.
items.solution: Test with real wallets on testnets. Use Synpress for E2E tests.

items.title: Hardcoding contract addresses
items.description: Makes deployment to different networks painful.
items.solution: Use environment variables or config files for addresses.

items.title: Using outdated libraries
items.description: Old versions of ethers/web3 have bugs and security issues.
items.solution: Keep dependencies updated. Consider migrating to viem/wagmi.

items.title: No error boundaries
items.description: One error crashes entire app instead of just affected component.
items.solution: Wrap components in error boundaries. Show fallback UI.

items.title: Ignoring TypeScript types
items.description: Using 'any' types leads to runtime errors.
items.solution: Use strict TypeScript. wagmi and viem have excellent types.

proTips: Most frontend exploits target the user, not the code. Think like a phisher.
Test with multiple wallets. MetaMask behavior differs from WalletConnect.
